questions.prompt:
Consider the following functions, defined for all real \(x\):
\[
f_1(x)=x,\qquad f_2(x)=x\cos x,\qquad f_3(x)=3e^{2x},\qquad f_4(x)=x-|x|.
\]
For each row below, answer Yes or No for every function. No justification is required in the historical question.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Does \(f(-x)=-f(x)\)? Give four answers in the order \(f_1,f_2,f_3,f_4\).
parts.answer: \(f_1:\text{ Yes},\ f_2:\text{ Yes},\ f_3:\text{ No},\ f_4:\text{ No}.\) The first two are odd. The exponential is not odd, and \(x-|x|\) is zero for every \(x\ge0\), so it cannot have origin symmetry.

parts.prompt: Does an inverse function exist?

questions.explanation: All sixteen classifications follow from parity, injectivity, periodicity, and continuity tests; the complete justification is given in the worked solution.
questions.workedSolution:
For oddness,
\[
f_1(-x)=-f_1(x),\qquad f_2(-x)=(-x)\cos(-x)=-x\cos x=-f_2(x),
\]
whereas \(f_3(x)=3e^{2x}\) is not odd and
\[
f_4(x)=x-|x|=\begin{cases}2x,&x<0,\\0,&x\ge0,\end{cases}
\]
is not odd. Thus (a) is **Yes, Yes, No, No**.

For inverses, \(f_1\) and the strictly increasing \(f_3\) are one-to-one. The function \(f_2\) is not one-to-one because \(f_2(\pi/2)=f_2(3\pi/2)=0\), and \(f_4\) is constant on \([0,\infty)\). Thus (b) is **Yes, No, Yes, No**.

No function is periodic: \(f_1,f_3,f_4\) plainly have no positive period, and the factor \(x\) prevents \(x\cos x\) from being periodic. Thus (c) is **No, No, No, No**.

The first three functions are continuous at \(0\). For \(f_4\),
\[
\lim_{x\to0^-}2x=0=\lim_{x\to0^+}0=f_4(0).
\]
Thus (d) is **Yes, Yes, Yes, Yes**.
questions.alternativeSolution:
\[
\begin{array}{c|cccc}
 & f_1&f_2&f_3&f_4\\\hline
\text{odd}&Y&Y&N&N\\
\text{invertible}&Y&N&Y&N\\
\text{periodic}&N&N&N&N\\
\text{continuous at }0&Y&Y&Y&Y
\end{array}
\]
This table follows directly from the parity identities, the two repeated-value counterexamples, and the piecewise form of \(f_4\).

questions.explanation: Differentiate the position, factor the velocity and acceleration, and use sign changes to distinguish a stop from a direction reversal.
questions.workedSolution:
\[
v(t)=x'(t)=12t^3-48t^2+48t=12t(t-2)^2,
\]
\[
a(t)=v'(t)=36t^2-96t+48=12(3t-2)(t-2).
\]
Hence the particle is at rest at \(t=0,2\). Since \((t-2)^2\ge0\), the sign of \(v\) is the sign of \(t\): \(v<0\) on \([-5,0)\) and \(v>0\) on \((0,2)\cup(2,5]\). Therefore direction changes only at \(t=0\); the double zero at \(t=2\) causes no reversal.

Acceleration first vanishes at \(t=2/3\) (the other zero is \(2\)), and
\[
v\!\left(\frac23\right)
=12\left(\frac23\right)\left(-\frac43\right)^2
=\frac{128}{9}.
\]
questions.alternativeSolution: A sign chart for \(v(t)=12t(t-2)^2\) gives the direction immediately: the squared factor never changes sign, so only crossing \(t=0\) reverses the motion. Then factor \(a(t)=12(3t-2)(t-2)\), select the first zero \(2/3\), and substitute into the factored velocity.

questions.prompt:
Let
\[
f(x)=\frac{1}{x}+\ln x,
\]
defined for
\[
e^{-1}\le x<e.
\]

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Determine the \(x\)-coordinates at which \(f\) has its absolute maximum and absolute minimum. Show the comparison.
parts.answer: Since \(f'(x)=\dfrac{x-1}{x^2}\), the function decreases on \([e^{-1},1]\) and increases on \([1,e)\). The absolute maximum is \(f(e^{-1})=e-1\), and the absolute minimum is \(f(1)=1\). The point \(x=e\) is excluded; \(\lim_{x\to e^-}f(x)=1+e^{-1}\) is not attained.

questions.explanation: The source uses a half-open domain. Derivative and endpoint analysis gives the extrema and shape, and direct integration gives the stated average value.
questions.workedSolution:
On the source domain \(e^{-1}\le x<e\),
\[
f'(x)=\frac{x-1}{x^2},\qquad f''(x)=\frac{2-x}{x^3}.
\]
Thus \(f\) decreases on \([e^{-1},1]\) and increases on \([1,e)\). Therefore
\[
f(e^{-1})=e-1\quad\text{(absolute maximum)},\qquad f(1)=1\quad\text{(absolute minimum)}.
\]
The excluded point \(x=e\) is not an endpoint candidate; \(\lim_{x\to e^-}f(x)=1+e^{-1}\).

Because \(x>0\), the graph is concave up on \((e^{-1},2)\), concave down on \((2,e)\), and has inflection point
\[
\left(2,\frac12+\ln2\right).
\]
The sketch begins at the closed point \((e^{-1},e-1)\), passes through the minimum \((1,1)\), changes concavity at \(x=2\), and approaches the open point \((e,1+e^{-1})\).

Finally,
\[
\int\left(\frac1x+\ln x\right)dx=\ln x+x\ln x-x,
\]
so
\[
\int_{e^{-1}}^e f(x)\,dx=2+\frac2e,\qquad e-e^{-1}=\frac{e^2-1}{e},
\]
and the average value is
\[
\frac{2+2/e}{e-e^{-1}}=\frac2{e-1}.
\]
It is the height of an equal-area rectangle over the base from \(e^{-1}\) to \(e\); omitting the single endpoint \(e\) does not change the integral.
questions.alternativeSolution:
The sign charts \(f':-\,,0,\,+\) at \(x=1\) and \(f'':+\,,0,\,-\) at \(x=2\) determine the entire sketch. As a check on the average value,
\[
\frac2{e-1}\left(e-e^{-1}\right)=2+\frac2e,
\]
which equals the definite integral.

questions.prompt:
The number of bacteria in a culture at time \(t\) is approximated by
\[
N(t)=1000\left(25+t e^{-t/20}\right),\qquad 0\le t\le100.
\]

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Find the largest and smallest numbers of bacteria during the interval, and state when they occur.
parts.answer:
\[N'(t)=1000e^{-t/20}\left(1-\frac{t}{20}\right).\]
The only interior critical time is \(t=20\). Compare
\[N(0)=25000,\quad N(20)=25000+\frac{20000}{e},\quad N(100)=25000+\frac{100000}{e^5}.\]
Thus the largest number is \(25000+\dfrac{20000}{e}\) at \(t=20\), and the smallest number is \(25000\) at \(t=0\).

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: At what time is the rate of change in the number of bacteria a minimum? Give the minimum rate.
parts.answer:
We minimize \(N'(t)\). Its derivative is
\[N''(t)=\frac{1000}{400}e^{-t/20}(t-40).\]
Therefore \(N'\) decreases until \(t=40\) and increases afterward. The minimum rate occurs at \(t=40\), and
\[N'(40)=-\frac{1000}{e^2}\ \text{bacteria per unit time}.\]

questions.explanation: Differentiate the population model to locate the population maximum, then differentiate the rate to locate its minimum.
questions.workedSolution:
\[
N'(t)=50(20-t)e^{-t/20}.
\]
Hence \(N\) increases to \(t=20\) and then decreases. Comparing the critical value and endpoints,
\[
N(20)=25000+\frac{20000}{e},\quad N(0)=25000,\quad
N(100)=1000(25+100e^{-5})>25000.
\]
Thus the greatest population is \(25000+20000/e\) at \(t=20\), and the least is \(25000\) at \(t=0\).

For the rate \(R=N'\),
\[
R'(t)=N''(t)=\frac52(t-40)e^{-t/20}.
\]
Therefore \(R\) decreases until \(t=40\) and increases afterward, so
\[
\min R=R(40)=50(-20)e^{-2}=-\frac{1000}{e^2}.
\]
questions.alternativeSolution: Let \(u=t/20\). Then \(N=25000+20000ue^{-u}\), whose variable factor has derivative \(e^{-u}(1-u)\), giving \(t=20\). Also \(N'=1000(1-u)e^{-u}\); differentiating with respect to \(u\) gives a factor \(u-2\), hence the minimum rate occurs at \(t=40\).

questions.prompt:
Let \(R\) be the region enclosed by the graphs
\[
y=x^2\qquad\text{and}\qquad y=2x.
\]

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Find the area of \(R\).
parts.answer:
The curves intersect where \(x^2=2x\), so \(x=0,2\). On this interval the line is above the parabola:
\[A=\int_0^2(2x-x^2)\,dx=\left[x^2-\frac{x^3}{3}\right]_0^2=\frac43.\]

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Find the volume obtained by revolving \(R\) about the \(y\)-axis.
parts.answer:
Using washers with respect to \(y\), \(0\le y\le4\), the outer radius is \(\sqrt y\) and inner radius is \(y/2\):
\[V=\pi\int_0^4\left[(\sqrt y)^2-\left(\frac y2\right)^2\right]dy
=\pi\int_0^4\left(y-\frac{y^2}{4}\right)dy=\frac{8\pi}{3}.\]
Equivalently, cylindrical shells give \(2\pi\int_0^2x(2x-x^2)\,dx\).

The curves meet at \(x=0,2\), and \(2x\ge x^2\) there. Hence

\[
V=2\pi\int_0^2x(2x-x^2)\,dx
=2\pi\left[\frac{2x^3}{3}-\frac{x^4}{4}\right]_0^2
=\frac{8\pi}{3},
\]

questions.prompt: An arched window has base width \(2b\) and height \(h\). The arch is either a parabolic arc or one half-cycle of a cosine curve. Its endpoints are \((-b,0)\) and \((b,0)\), and its highest point is \((0,h)\).

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Write an equation for the parabolic arch.
parts.answer:
By symmetry write \(y=h+Ax^2\). Using \(y(b)=0\) gives \(A=-h/b^2\). Thus
\[y=h\left(1-\frac{x^2}{b^2}\right),\qquad -b\le x\le b.\]

questions.explanation: Determine the symmetric parabolic and cosine models from the width and height, integrate each, and compare the exact areas.
questions.workedSolution:
With endpoints \((\pm b,0)\) and vertex \((0,h)\), the parabolic arch is
\[
y=h\left(1-\frac{x^2}{b^2}\right).
\]
The cosine arch with the same endpoints and height is
\[
y=h\cos\left(\frac{\pi x}{2b}\right).
\]
Their areas are
\[
A_P=\int_{-b}^{b}h\left(1-\frac{x^2}{b^2}\right)dx=\frac{4bh}{3},
\]
\[
A_C=\int_{-b}^{b}h\cos\left(\frac{\pi x}{2b}\right)dx=\frac{4bh}{\pi}.
\]
Since \(\pi>3\), \(A_P>A_C\); the parabolic window has the greater area.
questions.alternativeSolution:
Put \(x=bu\). Then
\[
A_P=bh\int_{-1}^{1}(1-u^2)\,du=\frac{4bh}{3},\qquad
A_C=bh\int_{-1}^{1}\cos\left(\frac{\pi u}{2}\right)du=\frac{4bh}{\pi}.
\]
The comparison is independent of the actual dimensions.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Find \(PQ\) as a function of \(r\), and find its limiting value as \(r\to\infty\).
parts.answer:
Since \(P=(r,0)\),
\[PQ=\left|r-\left(r-\frac{e^r+e^{-r}}{e^r-e^{-r}}\right)\right|=\left|\frac{e^r+e^{-r}}{e^r-e^{-r}}\right|.\]
For \(r\to\infty\), divide numerator and denominator by \(e^r\):
\[\lim_{r\to\infty}PQ=\lim_{r\to\infty}\frac{1+e^{-2r}}{1-e^{-2r}}=1.\]

questions.explanation: Differentiate the exponential curve, form the tangent at x equals r, solve for its x-intercept, and take the absolute horizontal distance.
questions.workedSolution:
Let
\[
f(x)=\frac12(e^x+e^{-x}),\qquad f'(x)=\frac12(e^x-e^{-x}).
\]
The graph is even, has minimum \((0,1)\), and is concave up everywhere because \(f''=f>0\).

At \(R=(r,f(r))\), the tangent is
\[
y-f(r)=f'(r)(x-r).
\]
Setting \(y=0\) gives
\[
x_Q=r-\frac{f(r)}{f'(r)}
=r-\frac{e^r+e^{-r}}{e^r-e^{-r}}
=r-\coth r,
\]
so \(Q=(r-\coth r,0)\). With \(P=(r,0)\),
\[
PQ=|x_Q-r|=|\coth r|.
\]
As \(r\to\infty\),
\[
PQ=\frac{1+e^{-2r}}{1-e^{-2r}}\longrightarrow1.
\]
questions.alternativeSolution:
Without hyperbolic notation,
\[
PQ=\left|\frac{e^{2r}+1}{e^{2r}-1}\right|.
\]
For \(r\to\infty\), divide by \(e^{2r}\) to obtain \((1+e^{-2r})/(1-e^{-2r})\to1\). The absolute value is essential when \(r<0\).

questions.prompt:
Consider the parabola
\[
y=x^2-2x+3.
\]
At the point \((2,3)\), let \(L\) be the line perpendicular to the tangent line. In the first quadrant, let \(R\) be the region lying below both the parabola and \(L\).

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Find an equation of the normal line \(L\) at \((2,3)\).
parts.answer:
The derivative is
\[
y'=2x-2,
\]
so the tangent slope at \(x=2\) is \(2\). The normal slope is therefore \(-\tfrac12\). Using \((2,3)\),
\[
y-3=-\frac12(x-2),
\qquad\boxed{y=4-\frac{x}{2}}.
\]

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Find the area of \(R\). Show the intersection and the integral setup.
parts.answer:
Solve the first-quadrant intersection:
\[
x^2-2x+3=4-\frac{x}{2}
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad 2x^2-3x-2=0,
\]
so \(x=2\) or \(x=-\tfrac12\). The relevant intersection is \(x=2\). The line meets the \(x\)-axis at \(x=8\). On \([0,2]\), the parabola is lower; on \([2,8]\), the line is lower. Thus
\[
A=\int_0^2(x^2-2x+3)\,dx+\int_2^8\left(4-\frac{x}{2}\right)\,dx.
\]
The two contributions are \(\tfrac{14}{3}\) and \(9\), so
\[
\boxed{A=\frac{41}{3}}.
\]

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Find the coordinates of every point where the tangent line is horizontal.
parts.answer:
For \(x\ne0\),
\[
f'(x)=\frac43x^{1/3}+\frac43x^{-2/3}=\frac{4(x+1)}{3x^{2/3}}.
\]
A horizontal tangent requires \(f'(x)=0\), so \(x=-1\). Since \(f(-1)=1-4=-3\), the point is
\[
\boxed{(-1,-3)}.
\]

questions.prompt: A right circular cone and a hemisphere have the same circular base, and the cone is inscribed in the hemisphere. The figure expands so that the combined surface area of the hemisphere and its base increases at a constant rate of \(18\) square inches per second. Find the rate at which the cone’s volume is changing when the common radius is \(4\) inches.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Express the total area in terms of \(r\), and find \(dr/dt\) when \(r=4\).
parts.answer:
The curved hemisphere has area \(2\pi r^2\), and its base has area \(\pi r^2\). Thus
\[
S=3\pi r^2.
\]
Differentiate:
\[
\frac{dS}{dt}=6\pi r\frac{dr}{dt}=18.
\]
At \(r=4\),
\[
\boxed{\frac{dr}{dt}=\frac{3}{4\pi}\text{ in/s}}.
\]

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Use the cone’s geometry to find \(dV/dt\) at that instant.
parts.answer:
For a cone inscribed in the hemisphere with the same base, the cone height equals the hemisphere radius: \(h=r\). Hence
\[
V=\frac13\pi r^2h=\frac13\pi r^3.
\]
Therefore
\[
\frac{dV}{dt}=\pi r^2\frac{dr}{dt}.
\]
At \(r=4\),
\[
\frac{dV}{dt}=\pi(16)\left(\frac{3}{4\pi}\right)=\boxed{12\text{ in}^3/\text{s}}.
\]

questions.prompt:
A particle moves along the \(x\)-axis so that, for \(t>0\), its position is
\[
x(t)=\sin(e^t).
\]

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Find the velocity and acceleration as functions of \(t\).
parts.answer:
By the chain and product rules,
\[
v(t)=x'(t)=e^t\cos(e^t),
\]
\[
a(t)=v'(t)=e^t\cos(e^t)-e^{2t}\sin(e^t).
\]

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: At what time does the particle first have zero velocity?
parts.answer:
Because \(e^t>0\), velocity is zero when \(\cos(e^t)=0\). Since \(t>0\), \(e^t>1\), and the first positive cosine zero reached is \(e^t=\frac{\pi}{2}\). Therefore
\[
\boxed{t=\ln\left(\frac{\pi}{2}\right)}.
\]

questions.prompt:
A parabola \(P\) is symmetric about the \(y\)-axis and passes through
\[
(0,0)\quad\text{and}\quad \left(b,e^{-b^2}\right),\qquad b>0.
\]
The region bounded by \(P\) and the horizontal line \(y=e^{-b^2}\) is revolved about the \(y\)-axis to form a solid \(F\).

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Write an equation for \(P\).
parts.answer:
A parabola symmetric about the \(y\)-axis with vertex at the origin has form \(y=ax^2\). Substituting \((b,e^{-b^2})\) gives
\[
a=\frac{e^{-b^2}}{b^2},
\]
so
\[
\boxed{y=\frac{e^{-b^2}}{b^2}x^2}.
\]

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Compute the volume of \(F\) as a function of \(b\).
parts.answer:
Using cylindrical shells, a vertical shell has radius \(x\) and height
\[
e^{-b^2}-\frac{e^{-b^2}}{b^2}x^2=e^{-b^2}\left(1-\frac{x^2}{b^2}\right).
\]
Thus
\[
V=2\pi e^{-b^2}\int_0^b x\left(1-\frac{x^2}{b^2}\right)dx
=\boxed{\frac{\pi}{2}b^2e^{-b^2}}.
\]
A washer integral with respect to \(y\) gives the same result.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: For what value of \(b\) is the volume maximum? Justify.
parts.answer:
Differentiate:
\[
V'(b)=\pi b e^{-b^2}(1-b^2).
\]
For \(b>0\), the only critical value is \(b=1\). The derivative is positive for \(0<b<1\) and negative for \(b>1\), so the volume is maximized at
\[
\boxed{b=1}.
\]
The maximum volume is \(\pi/(2e)\).

questions.prompt:
Given that
\[
\sin t\le t\qquad\text{for all }t\ge0,
\]
use repeated integration to prove that, for every \(x\ge0\),
\[
1-\frac{x^2}{2!}\le\cos x\le1-\frac{x^2}{2!}+\frac{x^4}{4!}.
\]

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Derive the lower bound \(1-\frac{x^2}{2}\le\cos x\).
parts.answer:
Integrate the given inequality from \(0\) to \(x\):
\[
\int_0^x\sin t\,dt\le\int_0^x t\,dt.
\]
Because \(x\ge0\), the order is preserved. Therefore
\[
1-\cos x\le\frac{x^2}{2},
\]
which rearranges to
\[
\boxed{1-\frac{x^2}{2}\le\cos x}.
\]

parts.answer:
From part (a), for every \(u\ge0\),
\[
\cos u\ge1-\frac{u^2}{2}.
\]
Integrate from \(0\) to \(t\):
\[
\sin t=\int_0^t\cos u\,du\ge t-\frac{t^3}{6}.
\]
Now integrate from \(0\) to \(x\):
\[
1-\cos x=\int_0^x\sin t\,dt
\ge\frac{x^2}{2}-\frac{x^4}{24}.
\]
Rearranging gives
\[
\boxed{\cos x\le1-\frac{x^2}{2}+\frac{x^4}{24}}
=\boxed{1-\frac{x^2}{2!}+\frac{x^4}{4!}}.
\]

questions.prompt:
Let
\[
f(x)=\ln x \quad (x>0),
\qquad g(x)=x^2-4 \quad (x\in\mathbb R).
\]
Define the compositions
\[
H(x)=f(g(x))
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
K(x)=g(f(x)).
\]

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Find the domain of \(H\).
parts.answer:
Since
\[
H(x)=\ln(x^2-4),
\]
we require \(x^2-4>0\). Thus \(x^2>4\), so
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{Dom}(H)=(-\infty,-2)\cup(2,\infty)}.
\]

parts.prompt: Find the range of \(H\).
parts.answer:
On its domain, \(x^2-4\) assumes every positive value. The natural logarithm maps \((0,\infty)\) onto all real numbers. Therefore

questions.prompt:
Let \(R\) be the region in the first quadrant that lies below both curves
\[
y=3x^2
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
y=\frac{3}{x},
\]
and to the left of the line \(x=k\), where \(k>1\).

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Find the area \(A\) of \(R\) as a function of \(k\).
parts.answer:
The curves meet where
\[
3x^2=\frac3x
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad x^3=1,
\]
so the first-quadrant intersection is \(x=1\). On \([0,1]\), the lower curve is \(3x^2\); on \([1,k]\), it is \(3/x\). Hence
\[
A(k)=\int_0^1 3x^2\,dx+\int_1^k\frac3x\,dx
=1+3\ln k.
\]
Thus
\[
\boxed{A(k)=1+3\ln k},\qquad k>1.
\]

parts.prompt: When the area of \(R\) is \(7\), find \(k\).
parts.answer:
Set the area equal to \(7\):
\[
1+3\ln k=7
\quad\Longrightarrow\quad
\ln k=2.
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{k=e^2}.
\]

Differentiate \(A=1+3\ln k\) with respect to time:
\[

5=\frac3{15}\frac{dk}{dt}.
\]
Hence
\[
\boxed{\frac{dk}{dt}=25\text{ units per second}}.
\]

questions.prompt:
Consider
\[
F(x)=\cos^2x+2\cos x
\]
over one complete period beginning with \(x=0\); use \(0\le x\le 2\pi\).

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Find all values of \(x\) in this period for which \(F(x)=0\).
parts.answer:
Factor:
\[
F(x)=\cos x(\cos x+2).
\]
Since \(\cos x=-2\) is impossible, we need \(\cos x=0\). Therefore
\[
\boxed{x=\frac\pi2,\;\frac{3\pi}{2}}.
\]

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Find all values of \(x\) in this period at which \(F\) has a minimum. Justify your answer.
parts.answer:
Complete the square:
\[
F(x)=(\cos x+1)^2-1.
\]
Because a square is nonnegative, the smallest possible value is \(-1\), attained when \(\cos x=-1\). In the stated period this occurs at
\[
\boxed{x=\pi},
\qquad F(\pi)=-1.
\]
This is the absolute minimum on the period.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: On what interval or intervals in this period is the graph concave up?
parts.answer:
Differentiate twice:
\[
F'(x)=-2\sin x(\cos x+1),
\]
\[
F''(x)=-2(2\cos^2x+\cos x-1)
=-2(2\cos x-1)(\cos x+1).
\]
Since \(\cos x+1\ge0\), the second derivative is positive when \(\cos x<\tfrac12\), except that it equals zero at the isolated point \(x=\pi\). Thus the graph is concave up throughout
\[
\boxed{\left(\frac\pi3,\frac{5\pi}{3}\right)}.
\]
The isolated zero of \(F''\) at \(x=\pi\) does not produce a change in concavity.

questions.prompt:
Find the area of the largest rectangle, with sides parallel to the coordinate axes, that can be inscribed in the region enclosed by
\[
f(x)=18-x^2
\qquad\text{and}\qquad
g(x)=2x^2-9.
\]

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Determine the dimensions and area of the largest such rectangle. Justify that the area is maximal.
parts.answer:
The curves intersect where
\[
18-x^2=2x^2-9,
\]
so \(x=\pm3\). By symmetry, let the vertical sides of the rectangle be \(x=\pm a\), where \(0\le a\le3\). Its width is \(2a\), and its height is
\[
(18-a^2)-(2a^2-9)=27-3a^2.
\]
Therefore
\[
A(a)=2a(27-3a^2)=54a-6a^3.
\]
Differentiate:
\[
A'(a)=54-18a^2=18(3-a^2).
\]
The positive critical value is \(a=\sqrt3\). Also,
\[
A''(a)=-36a<0
\]
at \(a=\sqrt3\), so this critical point gives a maximum. The dimensions are
\[
\text{width}=2\sqrt3,
\qquad
\text{height}=27-3(3)=18.
\]
Hence the largest area is
\[
\boxed{A_{\max}=36\sqrt3}.
\]

questions.prompt:
Let \(R\) be the first-quadrant region bounded by the \(x\)-axis and
\[
y=2x-x^2.
\]

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Find the volume generated when \(R\) is revolved about the \(x\)-axis.
parts.answer:
The curve meets the \(x\)-axis at \(x=0\) and \(x=2\). Using disks,
\[
V_x=\pi\int_0^2(2x-x^2)^2\,dx.
\]
Since
\[
(2x-x^2)^2=4x^2-4x^3+x^4,
\]
\[
V_x=\pi\left[\frac{4x^3}{3}-x^4+\frac{x^5}{5}\right]_0^2
=\boxed{\frac{16\pi}{15}}.
\]

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Find the volume generated when \(R\) is revolved about the \(y\)-axis.
parts.answer:
A washer solution remains within current AP Calculus AB methods. Write
\[
y=1-(x-1)^2,
\]
so for \(0\le y\le1\), the outer and inner radii are
\[
R(y)=1+\sqrt{1-y},
\qquad r(y)=1-\sqrt{1-y}.
\]
Therefore
\[
V_y=\pi\int_0^1\left[(1+\sqrt{1-y})^2-(1-\sqrt{1-y})^2\right]dy.
\]
The bracket simplifies to \(4\sqrt{1-y}\), so
\[
V_y=4\pi\int_0^1\sqrt{1-y}\,dy
=\boxed{\frac{8\pi}{3}}.
\]
Equivalently, cylindrical shells give \(2\pi\int_0^2x(2x-x^2)\,dx\).

questions.prompt:
A particle starts at the point \((5,0)\) at \(t=0\) and moves along the \(x\)-axis. For \(t>0\), its velocity is
\[
v(t)=\frac{t}{1+t^2}.
\]

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Determine the maximum velocity attained by the particle. Justify your answer.
parts.answer:
Differentiate:
\[
v'(t)=\frac{1-t^2}{(1+t^2)^2}.
\]
For \(t>0\), this derivative is positive on \((0,1)\) and negative on \((1,\infty)\). Thus the absolute maximum occurs at \(t=1\), with
\[
\boxed{v_{\max}=v(1)=\frac12}.
\]

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Determine the position of the particle at \(t=6\).
parts.answer:
Position equals initial position plus accumulated velocity:
\[
x(t)=5+\int_0^t\frac{s}{1+s^2}\,ds
=5+\frac12\ln(1+t^2).
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{x(6)=5+\frac12\ln37}.
\]

Although the velocity tends to zero, the position

x(t)=5+\frac12\ln(1+t^2)

\[
5+\frac12\ln(1+t^2)=500,
\]
so
\[
t=\sqrt{e^{990}-1},
\]
a finite but extremely large time. Thus \(
\boxed{\text{yes}}
\).

questions.prompt:
Let
\[
f(x)=|x|^{1/2}e^{-x^2}
\]
for all real numbers \(x\).

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Describe the symmetry of the graph of \(f\).
parts.answer:
Because \(|-x|=|x|\) and \((-x)^2=x^2\),
\[
f(-x)=|-x|^{1/2}e^{-(-x)^2}=|x|^{1/2}e^{-x^2}=f(x).
\]
Therefore \(f\) is even and its graph is symmetric about the \(y\)-axis:
\[
\boxed{f(-x)=f(x)}.
\]

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: On what intervals is \(f\) increasing?
parts.answer:
For \(x>0\),
\[
f(x)=x^{1/2}e^{-x^2},
\]
so
\[
f'(x)=e^{-x^2}\left(\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}-2x^{3/2}\right)
=\frac{e^{-x^2}(1-4x^2)}{2\sqrt{x}}.
\]
Thus \(f'(x)>0\) for \(0<x<\tfrac12\) and \(f'(x)<0\) for \(x>\tfrac12\). Since \(f\) is even, its derivative behavior reflects across the \(y\)-axis. Therefore \(f\) is increasing on
\[
\boxed{(-\infty,-\tfrac12)\cup(0,\tfrac12)}.
\]

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Sketch the graph, showing clearly its behavior near the origin, all maximum and minimum points, and its behavior for large \(|x|\).
parts.answer:
The function is nonnegative and even. It satisfies \(f(0)=0\), but the one-sided slopes become unbounded in magnitude, producing a sharp minimum at the origin. The critical points away from the origin are \(x=\pm\tfrac12\). At both points,
\[
f\left(\pm\frac12\right)
=\sqrt{\frac12}e^{-1/4}
=\frac{e^{-1/4}}{\sqrt2}.
\]
They are equal absolute maxima. Finally,
\[
\lim_{|x|\to\infty}|x|^{1/2}e^{-x^2}=0,
\]
so the graph approaches the \(x\)-axis from above on both ends. The feature list is therefore
\[
\boxed{\text{minimum }(0,0),\quad
\text{maxima }\left(\pm\frac12,\frac{e^{-1/4}}{\sqrt2}\right),\quad
f(x)\to0.}
\]

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Find the \(x\)-intercepts of the graph of \(f\).
parts.answer:
Factor the polynomial:
\[
4x^3-3x-1=(x-1)(4x^2+4x+1)=(x-1)(2x+1)^2.
\]
Thus the zeros are \(x=1\) and \(x=-\tfrac12\). Therefore the \(x\)-intercepts are
\[
\boxed{(1,0)\text{ and }\left(-\frac12,0\right)}.
\]
The intercept at \(x=-\tfrac12\) has even multiplicity, so the graph touches the axis there.

questions.prompt:
A particle starts at time \(t=0\) and moves on a number line so that its position at time \(t\) is
\[
x(t)=(t-2)^3(t-6),\qquad t\ge 0.
\]

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: When is the particle moving to the right?
parts.answer:
Differentiate the position:
\[
v(t)=x'(t)=3(t-2)^2(t-6)+(t-2)^3=4(t-2)^2(t-5).
\]
Since \((t-2)^2\ge0\), the sign is controlled by \(t-5\), except at the zeros. Therefore \(v(t)>0\) when
\[
\boxed{t>5}.
\]

The particle moves left until \(t=5\), then moves right. Thus its minimum position occurs at \(t=5\):

which is \(27\) units to the left of the origin.

questions.prompt:
Let
\[
f(x)=k\sin(kx),
\]
where \(k\) is a positive constant. Consider one positive arch of the graph, from \(x=0\) to \(x=\frac{\pi}{k}\).

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Find the area of the region bounded by one arch of the graph of \(f\) and the \(x\)-axis.
parts.answer:
The area is
\[
\int_0^{\pi/k} k\sin(kx)\,dx.
\]
Let \(u=kx\), so \(du=k\,dx\). Then
\[
\int_0^{\pi}\sin u\,du=[-\cos u]_0^{\pi}=2.
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{A=2}.
\]

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Find the area of the triangle formed by the \(x\)-axis and the tangent lines to this arch at the two points where the graph crosses the \(x\)-axis.
parts.answer:
Since
\[
f'(x)=k^2\cos(kx),
\]
the tangent at \(x=0\) is \(y=k^2x\), and the tangent at \(x=\pi/k\) is
\[
y=-k^2\left(x-\frac{\pi}{k}\right).
\]
They intersect at
\[
x=\frac{\pi}{2k},\qquad y=\frac{\pi k}{2}.
\]
The triangle has base \(\pi/k\) and height \(\pi k/2\). Thus
\[
A_\triangle=\frac12\left(\frac{\pi}{k}\right)\left(\frac{\pi k}{2}\right)
=\boxed{\frac{\pi^2}{4}}.
\]

questions.prompt:
A man has \(340\) yards of fencing for two separate fields. One field is a rectangle twice as long as it is wide, and the other is a square. The square must contain at least \(100\) square yards, and the rectangle must contain at least \(800\) square yards.

Let \(x\) be the width of the rectangular field.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Find the maximum and minimum possible values of \(x\).
parts.answer:
The rectangle has dimensions \(x\) by \(2x\), so its perimeter is \(6x\). Let the square side be \(s\). Using all the fencing,
\[
6x+4s=340,
\qquad s=85-\frac32x.
\]
The rectangle-area constraint gives
\[
2x^2\ge800\quad\Rightarrow\quad x\ge20.
\]
The square-area constraint gives \(s^2\ge100\). Since \(s>0\), \(s\ge10\), so
\[
85-\frac32x\ge10\quad\Rightarrow\quad x\le50.
\]
Hence
\[
\boxed{20\le x\le50}.
\]

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: What is the greatest total number of square yards that can be enclosed in the two fields? Justify your answer.
parts.answer:
The total area is
\[
A(x)=2x^2+s^2=2x^2+\left(85-\frac32x\right)^2
=\frac{17}{4}x^2-255x+7225.
\]
Because \(A''(x)=\tfrac{17}{2}>0\), this quadratic is concave up, so its maximum on the closed interval \([20,50]\) occurs at an endpoint.
\[
A(20)=800+55^2=3825,
\]
\[
A(50)=5000+10^2=5100.
\]
Therefore the greatest possible total area is
\[

questions.prompt:
Let
\[
y=2e^{\cos x}.
\]

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Calculate \(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\) and \(\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}\).
parts.answer:
By the chain rule,
\[
\frac{dy}{dx}=2e^{\cos x}(-\sin x)
=\boxed{-2e^{\cos x}\sin x}.
\]
Differentiate again:
\[
\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}
=-2\left[e^{\cos x}(-\sin x)\sin x+e^{\cos x}\cos x\right].
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{\frac{d^2y}{dx^2}=2e^{\cos x}(\sin^2x-\cos x)}.
\]

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Suppose \(x\) and \(y\) vary with time and \(y\) increases at a constant rate of \(5\) units per second. Find \(\dfrac{dx}{dt}\) when \(x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}\).
parts.answer:
Differentiate with respect to time:
\[
\frac{dy}{dt}=\frac{dy}{dx}\frac{dx}{dt}
=-2e^{\cos x}\sin x\frac{dx}{dt}.
\]
At \(x=\pi/2\), \(e^{\cos x}=1\) and \(\sin x=1\). Since \(dy/dt=5\),
\[
5=-2\frac{dx}{dt}.
\]
Thus
\[
\boxed{\frac{dx}{dt}=-\frac52\text{ units per second}}.
\]

questions.prompt:
The region \(R\) is bounded by
\[
xy=1,\qquad x=1,\qquad x=2,\qquad y=0.
\]
Equivalently, \(R\) lies under \(y=1/x\) for \(1\le x\le2\).

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Find the volume generated by revolving \(R\) about the \(x\)-axis.
parts.answer:
Using disks of radius \(1/x\),
\[
V=\pi\int_1^2\left(\frac1x\right)^2dx
=\pi\int_1^2x^{-2}\,dx.
\]
Thus
\[
V=\pi\left[-\frac1x\right]_1^2
=\pi\left(1-\frac12\right)
=\boxed{\frac\pi2}.
\]

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Find the volume generated by revolving \(R\) about the line \(x=3\).
parts.answer:
Using cylindrical shells, the radius is \(3-x\) and the height is \(1/x\):
\[
V=2\pi\int_1^2(3-x)\frac1x\,dx
=2\pi\int_1^2\left(\frac3x-1\right)dx.
\]
Therefore
\[
V=2\pi[3\ln x-x]_1^2
=2\pi(3\ln2-1).
\]
Hence
\[
\boxed{V=2\pi(3\ln2-1)}.
\]
A current-AB washer solution is also possible by integrating horizontally in two pieces.

From the derivative calculation,
\[
\boxed{f'(x)=4x}.
\]
Therefore
\[
f(x)=2x^2+C.
\]
Using \(f(1)=5\),
\[
2+C=5\quad\Rightarrow\quad C=3.
\]
Thus
\[
\boxed{f(x)=2x^2+3}.
\]

\[
f(a+b)-f(a)=2(a+b)^2-2a^2=4ab+2b^2,
\]

questions.prompt:
Let
\[
f(x)=x^3-6x^2+9x\qquad\text{and}\qquad g(x)=4.
\]

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Find the coordinates of the points common to the graphs of \(f\) and \(g\).
parts.answer:
Set \(f(x)=4\):
\[
x^3-6x^2+9x-4=0.
\]
The polynomial factors as
\[
(x-1)^2(x-4)=0.
\]
Thus \(x=1\) or \(x=4\), and the common points are
\[
\boxed{(1,4)\text{ and }(4,4)}.
\]

f(x)=x(x^2-6x+9)=x(x-3)^2.
\]

parts.answer:
Differentiate:
\[
f'(x)=3x^2-12x+9=3(x-1)(x-3).
\]
On \([0,2]\), the only interior critical point is \(x=1\). Evaluate the endpoints and this critical point:
\[
f(0)=0,\qquad f(1)=4,\qquad f(2)=2.
\]
The function is continuous, so it attains every value between its absolute minimum and maximum. Hence the range is
\[
\boxed{[0,4]}.

questions.prompt:
A particle moves on the \(x\)-axis. For \(t>0\), its acceleration is
\[
a(t)=\frac{t}{8}-\frac{1}{t^2}.
\]
When \(t=1\), the velocity is \(v=\frac{9}{16}\) and the position is \(s=\frac{25}{48}\).

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Find the velocity \(v\) in terms of \(t\).
parts.answer:
Integrate the acceleration:
\[
v(t)=\int\left(\frac{t}{8}-\frac1{t^2}\right)dt=\frac{t^2}{16}+\frac1t+C.
\]
Use \(v(1)=\frac9{16}\):
\[
\frac1{16}+1+C=\frac9{16}\quad\Rightarrow\quad C=-\frac12.
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{v(t)=\frac{t^2}{16}+\frac1t-\frac12},\qquad t>0.
\]

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Does the numerical value of the velocity ever exceed \(500\)? Explain.
parts.answer:
Yes. As \(t\to\infty\),
\[
v(t)=\frac{t^2}{16}+\frac1t-\frac12\longrightarrow\infty.
\]
Thus the velocity eventually exceeds any fixed positive number, including \(500\). For example,
\[
v(100)=625+0.01-0.5=624.51>500.
\]
Also, \(v(t)\to\infty\) as \(t\to0^+\) because of the \(1/t\) term.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Find the distance \(s\) from the origin at time \(t=2\).
parts.answer:
Integrate the velocity:
\[
s(t)=\frac{t^3}{48}+\ln t-\frac t2+C.
\]
Use \(s(1)=\frac{25}{48}\):
\[
\frac1{48}-\frac12+C=\frac{25}{48}\quad\Rightarrow\quad C=1.
\]
Therefore
\[
s(2)=\frac8{48}+\ln2-1+1=\frac16+\ln2.
\]
This value is positive, so the distance from the origin is
\[
\boxed{\frac16+\ln2}.
\]

questions.prompt:
The curve is defined implicitly by
\[
x+xy+2y^2=6.
\]

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Find an expression for the slope of the curve at any point \((x,y)\) where the slope is defined.
parts.answer:
Differentiate implicitly with respect to \(x\):
\[
1+y+x\frac{dy}{dx}+4y\frac{dy}{dx}=0.
\]
Collect the derivative terms:
\[
(x+4y)\frac{dy}{dx}=-(1+y).
\]
Thus
\[
\boxed{\frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{1+y}{x+4y}}.
\]

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Write an equation for the line tangent to the curve at \((2,1)\).
parts.answer:
At \((2,1)\),
\[
\frac{dy}{dx}=-\frac{1+1}{2+4}=-\frac13.
\]
Therefore the tangent line is
\[
y-1=-\frac13(x-2),
\]
or equivalently
\[
\boxed{x+3y=5}.
\]

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Find the coordinates of all other points on the curve where the slope equals the slope at \((2,1)\).
parts.answer:
Set the slope equal to \(-1/3\):
\[
-\frac{1+y}{x+4y}=-\frac13\quad\Rightarrow\quad x=3-y.
\]
Substitute into the curve:
\[
(3-y)+(3-y)y+2y^2=6,
\]
so
\[
y^2+2y-3=0=(y-1)(y+3).
\]
The solution \(y=1\) gives the original point. The other solution is \(y=-3\), giving \(x=6\). Hence the other point is
\[
\boxed{(6,-3)}.
\]

questions.prompt: Consider the line \(y=2x+b\) and the parabola \(y^2=4x\).

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Find the set of all values of \(b\) for which the two graphs intersect at two distinct points.
parts.answer:
Using \(x=y^2/4\) in the line gives
\[
y=\frac{y^2}{2}+b,
\]
so
\[
y^2-2y+2b=0.
\]
There are two distinct intersections exactly when the discriminant is positive:
\[
(-2)^2-4(1)(2b)>0\quad\Rightarrow\quad 4-8b>0.
\]
Thus
\[
\boxed{b<\frac12}.
\]

parts.answer:
For \(b=0\), the curves are \(y=2x\) and \(y=2\sqrt{x}\) in the bounded first-quadrant region. They meet at \(x=0\) and \(x=1\). Washers about the \(x\)-axis have outer radius \(2\sqrt{x}\) and inner radius \(2x\):
\[
V=\pi\int_0^1\left[(2\sqrt{x})^2-(2x)^2\right]dx
=4\pi\int_0^1(x-x^2)dx
=\boxed{\frac{2\pi}{3}}.
\]

questions.prompt:
For a fixed positive constant \(k\), consider the curve
\[
y=xe^{-kx}.
\]

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Find the coordinates of the absolute maximum point. Justify your answer.
parts.answer:
Differentiate:
\[
y'=e^{-kx}(1-kx).
\]
Because \(e^{-kx}>0\), the derivative is positive when \(x<1/k\) and negative when \(x>1/k\). Thus the function increases and then decreases, so its absolute maximum occurs at \(x=1/k\). The maximum value is
\[
y=\frac1k e^{-1}=\frac1{ke}.
\]
Therefore the maximum point is
\[
\boxed{\left(\frac1k,\frac1{ke}\right)}.
\]

parts.answer:
At a maximum point,
\[
x=\frac1k\quad\text{and}\quad y=\frac1{ke}.
\]
Since \(1/k=x\), eliminate \(k\):
\[
y=\frac{x}{e}.
\]
Because \(k>0\), we have \(x>0\). Thus the locus is the positive ray
\[
\boxed{y=\frac{x}{e},\quad x>0}.
\]

questions.prompt: A manufacturer pays \(x^2+5x+7\) dollars to produce \(x\) tons of an item. At production levels above \(3\) tons, additional workers increase the total cost by \(3(x-3)\) dollars. The item sells for \(13\) dollars per ton, and the plant capacity is \(10\) tons.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: What production level maximizes profit? Justify your answer.
parts.answer:
Revenue is \(R(x)=13x\). The profit is piecewise:
\[
P(x)=\begin{cases}
13x-(x^2+5x+7)=-x^2+8x-7,&0\le x\le3,\\
13x-[x^2+5x+7+3(x-3)]=-x^2+5x+2,&3<x\le10.
\end{cases}
\]
On \([0,3]\),
\[
P'(x)=8-2x>0,
\]
so profit increases up to \(x=3\). On \((3,10]\),
\[
P'(x)=5-2x<0,
\]
so profit decreases immediately after the threshold. The two formulas agree at the threshold, where
\[
P(3)=8.
\]
Therefore the maximizing production level is
\[
\boxed{3\text{ tons}}.
\]

questions.prompt: For \(k>0\), let \(A\) be the area of the first-quadrant region enclosed by the \(y\)-axis, the curve \(y=\tan x\), and the horizontal line \(y=k\).

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Find \(A\) as a function of \(k\).
parts.answer:
The line \(y=k\) meets \(y=\tan x\) at \(x=\arctan k\). Therefore
\[
A(k)=\int_0^{\arctan k}(k-\tan x)\,dx.
\]
Evaluate:
\[
A(k)=k\arctan k+\ln(\cos(\arctan k)).
\]
Since \(\cos(\arctan k)=1/\sqrt{1+k^2}\),
\[
\boxed{A(k)=k\arctan k-\frac12\ln(1+k^2)}.
\]

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: If the line \(y=k\) moves upward at \(\frac1{10}\) unit per second, find the rate at which \(A\) is changing when \(k=1\).
parts.answer:
Differentiate the area function. The endpoint terms cancel:
\[
\frac{dA}{dk}=\arctan k.
\]
By the chain rule,
\[
\frac{dA}{dt}=\frac{dA}{dk}\frac{dk}{dt}=\arctan(k)\left(\frac1{10}\right).
\]
At \(k=1\),
\[
\boxed{\frac{dA}{dt}=\frac{\pi}{40}}
\]
square units per second.

questions.prompt:
Given
\[
f(x)=|\sin x|,\qquad -\pi\le x\le\pi,
\]
and
\[
g(x)=x^2
\]
for all real values of \(x\).

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Sketch the graph of \(f\) on the given domain.
parts.answer: On \([-\pi,0]\), \(\sin x\le0\), so \(f(x)=-\sin x\). On \([0,\pi]\), \(f(x)=\sin x\). Thus the graph consists of two nonnegative sine arches, with included zeros at \(x=-\pi,0,\pi\) and maxima \(1\) at \(x=\pm\frac{\pi}{2}\).

parts.answer:
Because \(g(u)=u^2\),

H(x)=g(f(x))=(|\sin x|)^2=\boxed{\sin^2x}.
\]

parts.answer:
The composition uses the same allowed inputs as \(f\), because \(g\) is defined for every real input. Hence
\[
\operatorname{Dom}(H)=\boxed{[-\pi,\pi]}.
\]

parts.answer:
Differentiate:
\[

\]
At \(x=\frac{\pi}{4}\),

\]
Therefore the tangent line is

\boxed{y-\frac12=x-\frac{\pi}{4}}.
\]

questions.prompt:
Let
\[
P(x)=x^4+ax^3+bx^2+cx+d.
\]
The graph of \(y=P(x)\) is symmetric with respect to the \(y\)-axis, has a relative maximum at \((0,1)\), and has an absolute minimum at \((q,-3)\).

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Determine the values of \(a,b,c,d\), and use these values to write an expression for \(P(x)\).
parts.answer:
Symmetry about the \(y\)-axis makes \(P\) even, so the odd-power coefficients vanish:
\[
a=0,\qquad c=0.
\]
Because \((0,1)\) lies on the graph, \(d=P(0)=1\). Thus
\[
P(x)=x^4+bx^2+1.
\]
At a nonzero minimum coordinate \(q\),
\[
P'(q)=4q^3+2bq=2q(2q^2+b)=0,
\]
so \(b=-2q^2\). Also \(P(q)=-3\), so
\[
q^4+bq^2+1=-3.
\]
Substituting \(b=-2q^2\) gives \(1-q^4=-3\), hence \(q^4=4\), \(q^2=2\), and \(b=-4\). Therefore
\[
\boxed{a=0,\ b=-4,\ c=0,\ d=1},\qquad \boxed{P(x)=x^4-4x^2+1}.
\]

parts.answer:

\[
\boxed{q=\pm\sqrt2}.
\]

questions.prompt:
Let
\[
f(x)=kx^2+c.
\]

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Find \(x_0\) in terms of \(k\) such that the tangent lines at \((x_0,f(x_0))\) and \((-x_0,f(-x_0))\) are perpendicular.
parts.answer:
If \(k=0\), both tangent lines are horizontal, so no such perpendicular pair exists. For \(k
e0\), since \(f'(x)=2kx\), the two slopes at \(x_0\) and \(-x_0\) are \(2kx_0\) and \(-2kx_0\). Their product must be \(-1\):
\[
(2kx_0)(-2kx_0)=-1.
\]
Thus \(4k^2x_0^2=1\). One convenient choice is
\[
\boxed{x_0=\frac1{2k}},
\]
and the opposite choice merely interchanges the two tangent points.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Find the slopes of the tangent lines from part (a).
parts.answer:
Using \(x_0=1/(2k)\),
\[
2kx_0=1,\qquad -2kx_0=-1.
\]
Thus the slopes are
\[
\boxed{1\text{ and }-1}.
\]

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Find, in terms of \(k\) and \(c\), the coordinates of the point where the two tangent lines intersect.
parts.answer:
At either tangent point,
\[
f(x_0)=kx_0^2+c=\frac1{4k}+c.
\]
With \(x_0=1/(2k)\), the two tangent lines simplify to
\[
y=x+c-\frac1{4k},\qquad y=-x+c-\frac1{4k}.
\]
Equating them gives \(x=0\), and then
\[
y=c-\frac1{4k}.
\]
Therefore the intersection is
\[
\boxed{\left(0,c-\frac1{4k}\right)}.
\]

questions.prompt:
Let \(f\) be defined for all \(x>-5\) and satisfy
\[
f''(x)=\frac{1}{3\sqrt{x+5}}.
\]
The line tangent to the graph of \(f\) at \((4,2)\) has an angle of inclination of \(45^\circ\). Find an expression for \(f(x)\).

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Determine \(f(x)\), showing how both constants of integration are found.
parts.answer:
An inclination angle of \(45^\circ\) gives tangent slope
\[
f'(4)=\tan45^\circ=1.
\]
Integrate the second derivative:
\[
f'(x)=\frac23\sqrt{x+5}+C_1.
\]
Using \(f'(4)=1\),
\[
1=\frac23\sqrt9+C_1=2+C_1,
\]
so \(C_1=-1\). Integrate again:
\[
f(x)=\frac49(x+5)^{3/2}-x+C_2.
\]
Now use \(f(4)=2\):
\[
2=\frac49(9)^{3/2}-4+C_2=12-4+C_2,
\]
so \(C_2=-6\). Therefore
\[
\boxed{f(x)=\frac49(x+5)^{3/2}-x-6},\qquad x>-5.
\]

questions.prompt:
A ball is thrown from the origin. Its path is modeled by
\[
y=mx-\frac{1}{1000}e^{2m}x^2,
\]
where \(m>0\) is the slope of the path at the origin.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: For what value of \(m\) will the ball strike the horizontal axis at the greatest distance from the origin? Justify your answer.
parts.answer:
Set \(y=0\). Besides \(x=0\), the positive intercept is
\[
R(m)=1000me^{-2m}.
\]
Differentiate:
\[
R'(m)=1000e^{-2m}(1-2m).
\]
Since the exponential factor is positive, \(R'(m)>0\) for \(0<m<1/2\) and \(R'(m)<0\) for \(m>1/2\). Therefore the range is maximized at
\[
\boxed{m=\frac12}.
\]

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: For what value of \(m\) will the ball strike at the greatest height on a vertical wall located 100 feet from the origin?
parts.answer:
At the wall \(x=100\), the height is
\[
h(m)=100m-\frac{100^2}{1000}e^{2m}.
\]
Therefore
\[
h(m)=100m-10e^{2m}.
\]
Then
\[
h'(m)=100-20e^{2m}.
\]
Set \(h'(m)=0\):
\[
e^{2m}=5\quad\Rightarrow\quad m=\frac12\ln5.
\]
Moreover,
\[
h''(m)=-40e^{2m}<0,
\]
so this critical value gives the greatest wall height. Thus
\[
\boxed{m=\frac12\ln5}.
\]

questions.prompt:
Let
\[
f(x)=\tan x\qquad\text{and}\qquad g(x)=\sqrt2\cos x.
\]

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Find the coordinates of the point where the graphs of \(f\) and \(g\) intersect in \(0<x<\frac{\pi}{2}\).
parts.answer:
Set the functions equal:
\[
\tan x=\sqrt2\cos x.
\]
Multiplying by \(\cos x>0\) gives
\[
\sin x=\sqrt2\cos^2x=\sqrt2(1-\sin^2x).
\]
The admissible solution is \(\sin x=1/\sqrt2\), so \(x=\pi/4\). Then \(y=\tan(\pi/4)=1\). Hence the intersection is
\[
\boxed{\left(\frac\pi4,1\right)}.
\]

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Find the area of the region enclosed by the \(y\)-axis and the graphs of \(f\) and \(g\).
parts.answer:
On \([0,\pi/4]\), \(\sqrt2\cos x\) lies above \(\tan x\). Therefore
\[
A=\int_0^{\pi/4}\left(\sqrt2\cos x-\tan x\right)dx.
\]
Since \(\int-\tan x\,dx=\ln(\cos x)\),
\[
A=\left[\sqrt2\sin x+\ln(\cos x)\right]_0^{\pi/4}
=1+\ln\left(\frac1{\sqrt2}\right).
\]
Thus
\[
\boxed{A=1-\frac12\ln2}.
\]

questions.prompt: The rate of change of the number of bacteria in a culture is proportional to the number present. A laboratory culture had 10,000 bacteria initially, 20,000 bacteria at time \(t_1\) minutes, and 100,000 bacteria at time \(t_1+10\) minutes.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: In terms of \(t\) only, find the number of bacteria in the culture at any time \(t\geq0\).
parts.answer:
Proportional growth satisfies
\[
P'(t)=kP(t),\qquad P(t)=10000e^{kt}.
\]
The two observations give
\[
10000e^{kt_1}=20000,\qquad 10000e^{k(t_1+10)}=100000.
\]
Dividing the second equation by the first yields
\[
e^{10k}=5,\qquad k=\frac{\ln5}{10}.
\]
Therefore
\[
\boxed{P(t)=10000e^{(\ln5)t/10}=10000\,5^{t/10}}.
\]

questions.prompt:
Given the function
\[
f(x)=\ln(x^2-9).
\]

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Describe the symmetry of the graph of \(f\).
parts.answer: Because\[f(-x)=\ln((-x)^2-9)=\ln(x^2-9)=f(x),\]the function is even. Therefore its graph is \boxed{\text{symmetric about the }y\text{-axis}}.

parts.answer: The logarithm requires \(x^2-9>0\). Thus \(|x|>3\), and\[\boxed{\operatorname{Dom}(f)=(-\infty,-3)\cup(3,\infty)}.\]

parts.answer: Solve\[\ln(x^2-9)=0\iff x^2-9=1\iff x^2=10.\]Both solutions lie in the domain, so\[\boxed{x=\pm\sqrt{10}}.\]

questions.prompt:
A particle moves along the \(x\)-axis. Its position at time \(t\), for \(t\ge0\), is
\[
s(t)=\frac13t^3-3t^2+8t.
\]

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Show that at time \(t=0\) the particle is moving to the right.
parts.answer: The velocity is\[v(t)=s'(t)=t^2-6t+8=(t-2)(t-4).\]Hence \(v(0)=8>0\), so the particle is \boxed{\text{moving to the right at }t=0}.

questions.prompt:
The function \(f\) is defined for every real number by
\[
f(x)=2|x-1|x^2.
\]

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: What is the range of \(f\)?
parts.answer:
Because \(2|x-1|x^2\ge0\), and it equals \(0\) at \(x=0\) and \(x=1\), the minimum value is \(0\). Also \(f(x)\to\infty\) as \(x\to\pm\infty\). Therefore
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{Range}(f)=[0,\infty)}.
\]

parts.prompt: For what values of \(x\) is \(f'\) continuous?
parts.answer:
Write the function piecewise:
\[
f(x)=\begin{cases}2x^2-2x^3,&x<1,\\2x^3-2x^2,&x\ge1.\end{cases}
\]
Thus
\[
f'(x)=\begin{cases}4x-6x^2,&x<1,\\6x^2-4x,&x>1.\end{cases}
\]
At \(x=1\), the one-sided derivatives are \(-2\) and \(2\), so \(f'\) does not exist there. Hence \(f'\) is continuous on
\[
\boxed{(-\infty,1)\cup(1,\infty)}.
\]

questions.prompt:
Consider
\[
y=x+\sin x,\qquad -\frac{\pi}{2}\le x\le\frac{3\pi}{2}.
\]

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Find the coordinates of all maximum and minimum points on the given interval. Justify your answers.
parts.answer: \[y'=1+\cos x\ge0\]throughout the interval, with equality only at \(x=\pi\). The derivative does not change sign there, so the function is increasing across the entire interval. Hence the absolute minimum and maximum occur at the endpoints:\[\boxed{\left(-\frac\pi2,-\frac\pi2-1\right)}\quad\text{and}\quad\boxed{\left(\frac{3\pi}{2},\frac{3\pi}{2}-1\right)}.\]There is no interior relative extremum.

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Find the coordinates of all points of inflection on the given interval. Justify your answers.
parts.answer: \[y''=-\sin x.\]Its sign changes at \(x=0\) and \(x=\pi\): concave up on \((-\pi/2,0)\), down on \((0,\pi)\), and up on \((\pi,3\pi/2)\). Therefore the inflection points are\[\boxed{(0,0)\text{ and }(\pi,\pi)}.\]The point \((\pi,\pi)\) is a stationary inflection point because \(y'(\pi)=0\).

parts.answer: The graph increases from the absolute minimum at \((-\pi/2,-\pi/2-1)\) to the absolute maximum at \((3\pi/2,3\pi/2-1)\). It passes through \((0,0)\), has a horizontal tangent and inflection at \((\pi,\pi)\), and changes concavity at both \(0\) and \(\pi\).

questions.prompt:
The vertical line \(x=c\), where \(c>0\), intersects the cubic
\[
y=2x^3+3x^2-9
\]
at \(P\), and the parabola
\[
y=4x^2+4x+5
\]
at \(Q\).

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: If the tangent to the cubic at \(P\) is parallel to the tangent to the parabola at \(Q\), find \(c\).
parts.answer: The tangent slopes at \(x=c\) are\[m_P=6c^2+6c,\qquad m_Q=8c+4.\]Set them equal:\[6c^2+6c=8c+4\iff3c^2-c-2=0\iff(3c+2)(c-1)=0.\]Since \(c>0\),\[\boxed{c=1}.\]

questions.prompt:
Let \(R\) be the first-quadrant region bounded by
\[
\frac{x^2}{9}+\frac{y^2}{81}=1
\]
and
\[
3x+y=9.
\]Set up the requested integrals, but do not evaluate them.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Set up an integral for the area of \(R\), with an integrand in one variable.
parts.answer: The upper ellipse branch is \(y=3\sqrt{9-x^2}\), and the line is \(y=9-3x\). They meet at \(x=0\) and \(x=3\). Hence\[\boxed{A=\int_0^3\left[3\sqrt{9-x^2}-(9-3x)\right]dx}.\]

questions.prompt:
A differentiable function \(f\) satisfies, for all real \(x\) and \(h\),
\[
f(x+h)=e^h f(x)+e^x f(h),
\]
and
\[
f'(0)=2.
\]

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Show that \(f(0)=0\).
parts.answer: Set \(h=0\):\[f(x)=f(x)+e^x f(0).\]Therefore \(e^x f(0)=0\) for every real \(x\), and since \(e^x>0\),\[\boxed{f(0)=0}.\]

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Using the definition of \(f'(0)\), find \(\displaystyle\lim_{x\to0}\frac{f(x)}{x}\).
parts.answer: Because \(f(0)=0\),\[f'(0)=\lim_{x\to0}\frac{f(x)-f(0)}{x}=\lim_{x\to0}\frac{f(x)}x.\]Given \(f'(0)=2\), the limit is \boxed2.

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: Prove that there is a real number \(p\) such that \(f'(x)=f(x)+pe^x\) for every real \(x\).
parts.answer: For fixed \(x\), subtract \(f(x)\), divide by \(h\), and use the functional equation:\[\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}h=f(x)\frac{e^h-1}{h}+e^x\frac{f(h)}h.\]As \(h\to0\), the left side tends to \(f'(x)\), the first quotient tends to \(1\), and by part (b) the second quotient tends to \(2\). Hence\[f'(x)=f(x)+2e^x.\]This has the required form with a real constant \(p\).

questions.prompt:
Let \(f\) be the real-valued function defined by
\[
f(x)=\sqrt{1+6x}.
\]

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Give the domain and range of \(f\).
parts.answer:
The radicand must be nonnegative: \(1+6x\ge0\), so \(x\ge-\tfrac16\). The principal square root is nonnegative and assumes every nonnegative value. Therefore
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{Dom}(f)=\left[-\frac16,\infty\right),\qquad \operatorname{Range}(f)=[0,\infty)}.
\]

questions.prompt: Consider the hyperbola \[3x^2-y^2=23.\]

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: A point moves on the hyperbola \(3x^2-y^2=23\) so that its y-coordinate is increasing at a constant rate of \(4\) units per second. How fast is the x-coordinate changing when \(x=4\)?
parts.answer:
Implicit differentiation gives
\[
6x\frac{dx}{dt}-2y\frac{dy}{dt}=0,\qquad \frac{dx}{dt}=\frac{y}{3x}\frac{dy}{dt}.
\]
At \(x=4\), the hyperbola has \(y=\pm5\). Since \(dy/dt=4\),
\[
\frac{dx}{dt}=\frac{y}{3(4)}(4)=\frac y3.
\]
Thus the rate is \(\boxed{5/3}\) at \((4,5)\) and \(\boxed{-5/3}\) at \((4,-5)\). The source does not identify the branch, so it does not determine a unique rate.

questions.prompt:
Analyze
\[
y=e^{\sin x}\qquad\text{for}\qquad -\pi\le x\le2\pi.
\]

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Find all maximum and minimum points on the interval. Justify.
parts.answer:
\[
y'=e^{\sin x}\cos x.
\]
The interior critical points are \(x=-\pi/2,\pi/2,3\pi/2\). Their values are \(e^{-1},e,e^{-1}\), respectively. Endpoint values are \(1\). Therefore the absolute maximum is
\[
\boxed{(\pi/2,e)},
\]
and the absolute minima are
\[
\boxed{(-\pi/2,e^{-1})\quad\text{and}\quad(3\pi/2,e^{-1})}.
\]

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Sketch the graph on the stated interval.
parts.answer: The graph starts at \((-\pi,1)\), decreases to \((-\pi/2,e^{-1})\), rises to \((\pi/2,e)\), decreases to \((3\pi/2,e^{-1})\), and rises to \((2\pi,1)\). It remains positive and is symmetric about \(x=\pi/2\).

questions.prompt:
For a differentiable function \(f\), define
\[
f^*(x)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{f(x+h)-f(x-h)}{h}.
\]

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Find \(f^*(x)\) for \(f(x)=x^2+x\).
parts.answer:
\[
f(x+h)-f(x-h)=4xh+2h.
\]
Therefore
\[
f^*(x)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{4xh+2h}{h}=\boxed{4x+2}.
\]

parts.answer:
Using \(\cos(x+h)-\cos(x-h)=-2\sin x\sin h\),
\[
f^*(x)=-2\sin x\lim_{h\to0}\frac{\sin h}{h}=\boxed{-2\sin x}.
\]

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: State and justify the relationship between \(f^*\) and the usual derivative \(f'\).
parts.answer:
Rewrite the quotient as
\[
\frac{f(x+h)-f(x-h)}h=\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}h+\frac{f(x)-f(x-h)}h.
\]
For differentiable \(f\), both terms tend to \(f'(x)\). Consequently
\[
\boxed{f^*(x)=2f'(x)}.
\]

questions.prompt:
Let \(f(x)=\cos x\) for \(0\le x\le2\pi\), and let \(g(x)=\ln x\) for \(x>0\). Let \(S\) be the composition of \(g\) with \(f\):
\[
S(x)=g(f(x))=\ln(\cos x).
\]

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Find the domain of \(S\).
parts.answer:
The logarithm requires \(\cos x>0\). Within \([0,2\pi]\), this gives
\[
\boxed{\left[0,\frac\pi2\right)\cup\left(\frac{3\pi}{2},2\pi\right]}.
\]

parts.prompt: Find the range of \(S\).
parts.answer:
On the domain, \(0<\cos x\le1\). The value \(1\) is attained at \(x=0\) and \(x=2\pi\), while \(\cos x\to0^+\) at the inner boundaries. Hence
\[
\boxed{\operatorname{Range}(S)=(-\infty,0]}.
\]

questions.prompt: Consider the function \[f(x)=(x^2-1)^3\]defined for all real numbers \(x\).

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: For what values of \(x\) is \(f\) increasing?
parts.answer: \[f'(x)=6x(x^2-1)^2.\]Because \((x^2-1)^2\ge0\), the derivative is positive for \(x>0\) except for the isolated stationary point \(x=1\). The function is strictly increasing across that point, so \[\boxed{f\text{ is increasing on }(0,\infty)}.\]Equivalently, a derivative sign chart may list \((0,1)\cup(1,\infty)\) and then note that the monotonic behavior continues through \(x=1\).

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Find the coordinates of all relative maximum and relative minimum points. Justify.
parts.answer: The derivative is negative for \(x<0\) and positive for \(x>0\), so the sign changes from negative to positive at \(x=0\). Thus \[\boxed{(0,-1)\text{ is a relative minimum}.}\]At \(x=\pm1\), the derivative is zero but does not change sign. Therefore \[\boxed{\text{there is no relative maximum}.}\]

parts.label: (c)
parts.prompt: For what values of \(x\) is the graph of \(f\) concave upward?
parts.answer: \[f''(x)=6(x^2-1)(5x^2-1).\]This product is positive when both factors have the same sign. Therefore the graph is concave upward on \[\boxed{(-\infty,-1)\cup\left(-\frac1{\sqrt5},\frac1{\sqrt5}\right)\cup(1,\infty)}.\]

parts.label: (d)
parts.prompt: Using the information from the previous parts, sketch the graph of \(f\).
parts.answer: The graph is even, has an absolute/relative minimum at \((0,-1)\), crosses the x-axis with horizontal tangents at \((\pm1,0)\), has inflection points at \(x=\pm1\) and \(x=\pm1/\sqrt5\), and rises to \(+\infty\) as \(x\to\pm\infty\).

questions.prompt: Let \[f(x)=e^{x/2}.\]Let \(R\) be the region bounded by the line \(y=e\), the graph of \(f\), and the \(y\)-axis.

parts.label: (a)
parts.prompt: Find the area of \(R\).
parts.answer: The curves meet when \(e^{x/2}=e\), so \(x=2\). Hence \[A=\int_0^2\left(e-e^{x/2}\right)\,dx=\left[ex-2e^{x/2}\right]_0^2=\boxed{2}.\]

parts.label: (b)
parts.prompt: Find the volume generated when \(R\) is revolved about the \(x\)-axis.
parts.answer: Using washers, the outer radius is \(e\) and the inner radius is \(e^{x/2}\): \[V=\pi\int_0^2\left(e^2-e^x\right)\,dx=\pi\left[ e^2x-e^x\right]_0^2=\boxed{\pi(e^2+1)}.\]
